red.focus: Turn a client's story into a legal-rights question
red.summary: Start legal analysis by asking who claims protection, against whom, and under what rule. Learn to separate the client's experience from the legal elements the decision maker must test.
checklist: I can identify the claimant and respondent
I can state the protected interest and alleged interference
I can separate a legal claim from a moral complaint

sections.title: Listen Before You Label
sections.body_md: A client says, 'My boss treated me unfairly.' The word unfairly matters, but does not itself identify the law violated. Ask what happened, when, who acted, what the client lost, and which legal protections may apply. The right at issue could arise from contract, anti-discrimination law, workplace safety rules or another source. Beginning with careful listening avoids forcing a complex life into an inaccurate legal category. It also helps the client feel heard before advice becomes technical.

sections.title: Name the Legal Relationship
sections.body_md: A rights claim generally identifies a person or entity protected and another person or institution under a corresponding duty or restriction. Constitutional rights may protect against state action; statutory rights may regulate private employers; contractual rights can bind defined parties. The same event can involve more than one relation. A beginner should write one clear sentence: 'Under [source], [claimant] may require [respondent] to [act or refrain] if [conditions].' This format turns a vague grievance into a testable issue.

sections.title: Rights Are Not Unlimited Promises
sections.body_md: A law may recognize freedom of expression yet permit specified limits. A consumer may have protection against misleading conduct but still need to show particular elements. Knowing the name of a right is therefore not enough. Identify the rule's trigger, exceptions, defenses and available remedy. A reliable legal adviser avoids saying 'you have a right' when the actual question is whether this client's facts satisfy the governing conditions. That precision protects the client's choices.

yellow.summary: Develop a claim by connecting the right's elements to identified facts. Understand why a legal entitlement often has limits and corresponding obligations.
checklist: I can decompose an entitlement into legal elements
I can distinguish conditions from exceptions
I can identify who bears the relevant proof burden

sections.title: Elements Build the Claim
sections.body_md: Suppose a renter asserts a statutory right to notice before eviction. The lawyer must find the statutory definition of tenancy, the type and period of notice, any permitted grounds, and the procedure used. Each requirement is a component of the claim. A useful element chart links the precise rule to a factual proposition and evidence. This separates what the client believes from what the tribunal needs to find under the law.

sections.title: Exceptions Matter
sections.body_md: A statute may grant a right subject to emergency exceptions, specified exclusions or time limits. A defendant may assert an affirmative defense rather than deny the claimant's basic elements. Those distinctions shape pleading and proof. For example, a particular consent exception may be invoked only under certain conditions. The lawyer should avoid stating the general protection so broadly that it erases the legislature's limits. Good advice identifies both the ordinary rule and the exception that might change the outcome.

sections.title: Proof Shapes Practical Rights
sections.body_md: An entitlement may be valid in principle but difficult to enforce without documents, witnesses or accessible procedures. Burdens of production and persuasion can be assigned differently by law, and the outcome may depend on the proof standard. A skilled legal analyst prepares an evidence map for each element and defense. That method makes it possible to tell a client precisely what is known, what is uncertain, and which fact would most change the case.

orange.focus: Resolve competing rights in hard cases
orange.summary: Analyze facts where several people can assert plausible legal protections. Construct a transparent argument that identifies the governing test rather than assuming one right automatically defeats another.
checklist: I can identify a genuine collision between rights
I can apply the jurisdiction's balancing or priority rule
I can explain least-restrictive alternatives where relevant

sections.title: Two People Can Both Have Claims
sections.body_md: A reporter investigates a public official, while the official seeks protection against disclosure of intimate medical details. Expression and privacy may both be legally relevant. Neither label automatically wins. The lawyer must find the jurisdiction's applicable test, identify the public interest, examine the character of the information, and consider harm. Some systems use proportionality or balancing; others give stronger categorical protection. A persuasive argument must be anchored in the actual law, not a preferred abstract ranking.

sections.title: The Facts Move the Balance
sections.body_md: Publication of a public budget decision is different from publication of a person's unrelated medical record. The difference matters because the asserted public interest and intrusion are not identical. A good argument explains which factual features are legally material under the governing test. If the law asks whether a restriction is necessary, the lawyer should evaluate alternatives rather than merely repeat 'important right.' Careful comparison preserves both interests while showing why the rule yields a particular result.

sections.title: Build the Best Counterargument
sections.body_md: Rights litigation often fails when counsel assumes opponents have no serious claim. Identify the strongest adverse authority and the factual point most favorable to the other side. Then answer it with the source, distinction or principle that genuinely supports the client's position. If the result is uncertain, explain that. This method produces stronger advocacy and better client advice because it anticipates the decision maker's concern instead of treating the conflict as a morality play.

black.focus: Develop a coherent theory of contested legal rights
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate why some rights deserve priority and who is entitled to make that judgment. Make legal theory serve accurate interpretation and human protection rather than mere abstraction.
checklist: I can distinguish text-based interpretation from moral argument
I can evaluate institutional limits in rights adjudication
I can defend a principled account of right-conflicts under uncertainty

sections.title: Rights Language Can Hide Theory
sections.body_md: A constitutional guarantee of liberty may be interpreted through text, structure, history, precedent and competing moral accounts. A decision maker's choice among these methods can shape outcomes. A doctoral argument must identify which approaches are authorized by the system and why any moral reasoning should influence interpretation. Merely calling a favored result 'fundamental' does not demonstrate legal authority. The aim is to make the path from sources to conclusion visible to readers who disagree.

sections.title: Priority Has Institutional Consequences
sections.body_md: Courts may protect minorities against majoritarian rules, but judges also hold coercive power and limited democratic accountability. Legislatures may bring information and public deliberation, but can overlook unpopular groups. A rights theory must explain which institution should decide, what factual record it needs, and how decisions can be corrected. The best approach does not assume either judicial supremacy or legislative control solves every conflict. It defends the procedural structure under which substantive rights are vindicated.

sections.title: A Great Lawyer Protects the Person
sections.body_md: A rights claim can affect freedom, family, safety and a client's ability to live with dignity. Counsel should communicate complex tests in terms the person understands, present choices honestly, and avoid using a vulnerable client as a vehicle for an attractive test case without consent. Doctoral legal mastery includes recognizing the tension between doctrinal reform and individual welfare. A sophisticated legal theory is worthwhile when it helps people understand, assert and protect their rights in the real world.
